items.rationale: The difference is who owns the control flow: in a workflow, code written in advance decides the steps and their order; in an agent, the model decides what to do next, step by step. Counting model calls (a) or tools (c) does not tell them apart, since workflows can use both, and a workflow can contain a model (d).

The code fixes the steps and their order, so the code owns the control flow and this is a workflow, even though it uses a tool and a model call. Using a tool or a model (a, b) does not make a system an agent; the model has no say over what happens next. The number of calls (d) is not the test.

The agent makes 4 + 1 = 5 model calls, which is 10 cents. The workflow makes 2 calls, which is 4 cents. The difference is 6 cents. An answer of 8 counts only the tool requests and misses the final-answer call.

Booking with known machine, date and time has steps that are the same every time, so code can run them in a fixed order, cheaply and predictably. The other three are open-ended: the steps depend on what is found along the way, which is where an agent earns its extra cost.

items.answer: When the steps are known in advance, code can run them with fewer model calls, so it costs less and behaves predictably.
accepted: It is cheaper because it needs fewer model calls.
It costs less and is more predictable than an agent.
It is cheaper and more reliable because the steps are fixed.
The model does not need to decide the steps, so there are fewer model calls and lower cost.
It is predictable and easier to test.
items.rationale: Any one of lower cost (fewer model calls), predictability or reliability, or ease of testing earns full credit, given that the steps are fixed. Claiming a workflow is smarter or more capable than an agent is wrong.

items.answer: Flexibility: it cannot adapt its steps to a request it was not built for.
accepted: The ability to adapt to unexpected requests
The model cannot choose different steps for different requests
It can't handle open-ended tasks where the steps are not known in advance
items.rationale: A workflow's steps are fixed in code, so it cannot choose a different path when a request does not fit; that flexibility is what an agent adds, at the cost of more model calls and less predictability. Answers about accuracy or intelligence do not follow from the choice.
